title: Structural insights into the binding potential of natural therapeutic leads as antiviral agents against human Metapneumovirus nucleoprotein
abstract: Human metapneumovirus (hMPV), a member of the family Pneumoviridae and the genus Metapneumovirus, is a prevalent cause of respiratory tract infections, leading to severe complications and even death. As of now, there are no approved specific antiviral drugs or vaccines for hMPV, underscoring the need for potential therapeutic candidates. Hence, the present study employed a structure-based virtual screening (SBVS) of prepared ligands from CMNPD and SPECS databases against the hMPV nucleoprotein. Multi-level precision screening identified CMNPD3066, CMNPD12667, CMNPD25748, SPECS-AE-765, and SPECS-AP-123 as the top computationally prioritized compounds. These compounds demonstrated favourable predicted interactions with the docking scores ranging from -9.8 to -7.5 kcal/mol, and post-docking MMGBSA binding free energies ranging from -74.02 to -54.81 kcal/mol. Further, ADME/T evaluation predicted that these candidates were not involved in the violation of Lipinski's rule of five (Ro5) and all demonstrated favourable pharmacokinetic profiles. Subsequent 500 ns molecular dynamics simulations (MDS) and essential dynamics (ED) analyses, including principal component analysis (PCA) and free energy landscape (FEL) mapping, revealed the conformational stability of the nucleoprotein-ligand complexes throughout the simulation period. Collectively, the study concludes that the identified hit molecules are promising binding candidates for therapeutic development against hMPV and warrant further experimental and clinical validation.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to identify potential antiviral agents against human metapneumovirus (hMPV) by employing structure-based virtual screening of ligands from CMNPD and SPECS databases against the hMPV nucleoprotein. The research highlights the need for specific therapeutic candidates due to the lack of approved antiviral drugs or vaccines for hMPV. The study identified five compounds as top computational leads, which showed favorable predicted interactions with docking scores ranging from -9.8 to -7.5 kcal/mol and binding free energies from -74.02 to -54.81 kcal/mol. ADME/T evaluation suggested these compounds adhered to Lipinski's rule of five and had favorable pharmacokinetic profiles. Molecular dynamics simulations confirmed the conformational stability of the nucleoprotein-ligand complexes. The findings suggest these compounds are promising candidates for therapeutic development against hMPV, warranting further experimental and clinical validation. The study's results are based on computational methods, which may have limitations in real-world applicability.

abstract_zh: 人偏肺病毒 (hMPV) 是肺病毒科和间质肺病毒属的成员,是呼吸道感染的常见原因,可导致严重并发症甚至死亡。截至目前,尚无批准用于 hMPV 的特定 抗病毒药物 药物或 疫苗,这凸显了对潜在治疗候选药物的需求。因此,本研究采用基于结构的虚拟筛选 (SBVS),对来自 CMNPD 和 SPECS 数据库的 hMPV 核蛋白制备配体进行分析。多级精密筛选将 CMNPD3066、CMNPD12667、CMNPD25748、SPECS-AE-765 和 SPECS-AP-123 确定为计算优先级最高的化合物。这些化合物表现出良好的预测相互作用,对接分数范围为-9.8至-7.5 kcal/mol,对接后MMGBSA结合自由能范围为-74.02至-54.81 kcal/mol。此外,ADME/T 评估预测这些候选药物不会违反 Lipinski 的五法则 (Ro5),并且均表现出良好的药代动力学特征。随后的 500 ns 分子动力学模拟 (MDS) 和基本动力学 (ED) 分析,包括主成分分析 (PCA) 和自由能图谱 (FEL) 映射,揭示了整个模拟期间核蛋白-配体复合物的构象稳定性。总的来说,该研究得出的结论是,所鉴定的命中分子是针对 hMPV 治疗开发的有希望的结合候选分子,并值得进一步的实验和临床验证。

title: Cardiac Complications of Infections Due to Respiratory Syncytial Virus and Human Metapneumovirus: A Systematic Review and Pooled Analysis of Clinical Features
abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and human metapneumovirus (hMPV) are major causes of respiratory tract infections across different age groups. Although primarily regarded as respiratory pathogens, both viruses have been associated with cardiac complications, whose clinical spectrum remains incompletely characterized. We systematically reviewed published cases of RSV- and hMPV-associated cardiac involvement and compared their clinical characteristics and outcomes. PubMed, Scopus, and EMBASE were systematically searched for reports describing cardiac complications associated with laboratory-confirmed RSV or hMPV infection. Individual patient data were pooled and analyzed using descriptive and univariate analyses. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify characteristics associated with hMPV versus RSV diagnosis, while multiple correspondence analysis (MCA) was performed to explore multivariate patterns of clinical presentation. Age-stratified sensitivity analyses were additionally performed. Overall, 102 cases were included, comprising 71 RSV (69.6%) and 31 hMPV (30.4%). hMPV cases were significantly older than RSV cases (41.5 years, interquartile range 3.5–63.0 vs. 1.5 years, interquartile range 0.2–31.0; p

title: High Conservation of the Human Metapneumovirus Fusion Protein in Contemporary Global Sequences Supports Its Continued Relevance for Therapeutic and Prophylactic Consideration
abstract: Human metapneumovirus (hMPV) is associated with severe disease in young children, older adults, and medically high-risk individuals. The hMPV F protein is highly immunogenic and a well-established target of neutralizing antibodies. In-depth hMPV surveillance data remain limited and may provide valuable insight into therapeutic development. Here we assembled a contemporary dataset of F gene sequences acquired from hMPV-positive nasal swab specimens collected between 2022 and 2023, together with contemporary F gene sequences from public surveillance databases, collected between 2017 and 2025. All sequences were subtyped and evaluated for residue-level similarity to reference alleles. Of 724 sequences in the combined contemporary dataset, A2 was the most predominant subtype accounting for nearly half of all sequences (50.83%). The mean F gene sequence similarity to reference alleles was 99.90%, 99.95%, and 99.84% for A2, B1, and B2, respectively; the least conserved residues were the stalk residue 518 for A2 (88.52% similarity to reference allele); BinD residue 450 for B1 (96.60% similarity); and site III residue 36 for B2 (77.88% similarity). Structural analysis showed that observed mutations were predominantly surface-exposed, with no evidence of novel N-linked glycosylation sequons, and were not predicted to significantly alter F protein structure. Overall, these findings indicate that the F protein is highly conserved across subtypes, with sequence variation unlikely to result in meaningful structural differences, thereby supporting development of F-targeted therapeutics against hMPV infection.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the conservation of the human metapneumovirus (hMPV) fusion (F) protein across contemporary global sequences to support its use in therapeutic and prophylactic development. The dataset included 724 F gene sequences from nasal swab specimens collected between 2022 and 2023, alongside sequences from public databases spanning 2017 to 2025. The most prevalent subtype was A2, accounting for 50.83% of sequences. Sequence similarity to reference alleles was high, with mean values of 99.90%, 99.95%, and 99.84% for A2, B1, and B2, respectively. Structural analysis revealed that mutations were primarily surface-exposed and unlikely to alter the F protein's structure. These findings suggest that the F protein remains a viable target for interventions against hMPV infection. However, the study's reliance on surveillance data without direct functional validation limits the strength of the evidence, which is considered moderate.

abstract_zh: 人偏肺病毒 (hMPV) 与幼儿、老年人和医学高危人群的严重疾病相关。hMPV F 蛋白具有高度免疫原性,是中和抗体的公认靶点。深入的 hMPV 监测 数据仍然有限,但可能为治疗开发提供有价值的见解。在这里,我们组装了从 2022 年至 2023 年收集的 hMPV 阳性鼻拭子标本中获取的当代 F 基因序列数据集,以及来自 2017 年至 2025 年期间收集的公共 监测 数据库的当代 F 基因序列。所有序列均进行了亚型分类,并评估了与参考等位基因的残基水平相似性。在合并的当代数据集中的 724 个序列中,A2 是最主要的亚型,占所有序列的近一半 (50.83%)。A2、B1 和 B2 与参考等位基因的平均 F 基因序列相似性分别为 99.90%、99.95% 和 99.84%;最不保守的残基是 A2 的茎残基 518(与参考等位基因的相似性为 88.52%);B1 的 BinD 残基 450(96.60% 相似性);B2 的位点 III 残基 36(77.88% 相似性)。结构分析表明,观察到的 突变 主要是表面暴露的,没有新的 N 连接糖基化序列的证据,并且预计不会显着改变 F 蛋白结构。总体而言,这些发现表明 F 蛋白在不同亚型中高度保守,序列变异不太可能导致有意义的结构差异,从而支持针对 hMPV 感染的 F 靶向疗法的开发。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 人偏肺病毒 (hMPV) 与幼儿、老年人和医学高危人群的严重疾病相关。该研究旨在评估 hMPV F 蛋白在当代全球序列中的保守性,以支持其与治疗和预防开发的相关性。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究汇集了 2022 年至 2023 年期间收集的 hMPV 阳性鼻拭子标本中的 F 基因序列的当代数据集,以及 2017 年至 2025 年公共 监测 数据库中的序列。该数据集包括 724 个序列,其中 A2 是最主要的亚型。
analysis_zh.methods: 对所有序列进行亚型分类并评估与参考等位基因的残基水平相似性。进行结构分析以评估观察到的 突变 对 F 蛋白结构的影响,重点关注表面暴露区域和潜在的 N 连接糖基化位点。
analysis_zh.main_results: 在合并的当代数据集中的 724 个序列中,A2 是最主要的亚型,占所有序列的近一半 (50.83%)。A2、B1 和 B2 与参考等位基因的平均 F 基因序列相似性分别为 99.90%、99.95% 和 99.84%。确定了每个亚型的最不保守的残基。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 观察到的 突变 主要是表面暴露的,并且没有引入新的 N 连接糖基化序列,表明它们不太可能显着改变 F 蛋白结构。这支持了 F 蛋白作为治疗靶标的持续相关性。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现表明,F 蛋白在 hMPV 亚型中高度保守,这可能为针对 hMPV 感染的靶向治疗药物和 疫苗 的开发提供信息。高度的序列相似性也表明现有的干预措施可能对当前菌株仍然有效。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究依赖于公开的 监测 数据,这可能会引入收集方法和代表性的可变性。由于依赖序列数据而没有直接的功能或临床验证,证据的强度中等。

title: Emerging Trends in the Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Management of Human Metapneumovirus-Associated Respiratory Infections
abstract: Introduction: Human Metapneumovirus is a significant respiratory pathogen causing infections across all age groups, particularly in young children, immunocompromised individuals, and the elderly. Despite its clinical relevance, there are currently no approved vaccines or specific antiviral treatments for Human Metapneumovirus, necessitating further research into therapeutic and preventive strategies. Methods: A systematic literature review was conducted using peer-reviewed journals, clinical trials, and recent studies focusing on Human Metapneumovirus infection. Data were extracted and analyzed to evaluate the effectiveness of antiviral therapies, monoclonal antibodies, immunomodulators, and vaccine candidates. Results: Studies indicate that Human Metapneumovirus primarily targets the respiratory epithelium, triggering immune responses that contribute to both viral clearance and disease pathogenesis. Investigational therapies, including fusion inhibitors and protease inhibitors, show promise but require further validation. Immunomodulatory agents and herbal remedies may offer supportive benefits, but their efficacy against Human Metapneumovirus remains unproven. Advances in vaccine development are ongoing, with several candidates in preclinical and early clinical stages. Discussion: HMPV continues to pose a substantial public health burden due to its seasonal outbreaks, clinical similarity to other respiratory viruses, and absence of specific therapies. The virus evades immune responses via multiple mechanisms, contributing to disease severity, particularly in vulnerable populations. Although supportive care is currently the mainstay, emerging antivirals and vaccines may offer future solutions. Improved diagnostic access, public awareness, and targeted research are essential for controlling HMPV infections. Conclusion: Human Metapneumovirus continues to pose a public health challenge due to the lack of targeted treatments and vaccines. Ongoing research into antiviral agents, monoclonal antibodies, and vaccines is critical for effective disease management. Further clinical trials are needed to establish safe and effective therapeutic options.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the pathogenesis, diagnosis, and management of human metapneumovirus (HMPV) infections, emphasizing its impact on vulnerable populations. The evidence highlights the virus's targeting of respiratory epithelium and the immune responses it triggers. While investigational therapies like fusion and protease inhibitors show promise, their efficacy remains unproven. Vaccine development is ongoing, with several candidates in early stages. The review underscores the need for further clinical trials, improved diagnostics, and public awareness to address the public health burden of HMPV. Despite the lack of specific treatments and vaccines, the study suggests that emerging antivirals and vaccines may offer future solutions.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 人偏肺病毒 (HMPV) 感染和疾病。该综述重点关注 发病机制、诊断 和 HMPV 相关呼吸道感染的管理,特别是幼儿、免疫功能低下者和老年人等弱势群体。
elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 通过系统性文献综述,检索同行评议期刊、临床试验及近期研究,重点关注人偏肺病毒感染。提取并分析数据,以评估抗病毒药物、单克隆抗体、免疫调节剂及疫苗候选物的有效性。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 人偏肺病毒 主要针对呼吸道上皮,触发 免疫应答,从而有助于病毒清除和疾病 发病机制。包括融合抑制剂和蛋白酶抑制剂在内的研究疗法显示出希望,但需要进一步验证。免疫调节剂和草药可能会提供支持性益处,但它们对抗 HMPV 的功效尚未得到证实。疫苗 的开发正在进行中,有几个候选药物处于临床前和早期临床阶段。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 该病毒通过多种机制逃避 免疫应答,导致疾病严重化,特别是在弱势群体中。尽管目前支持性护理是主流,但新兴的 抗病毒药物 和 疫苗 可能会提供未来的解决方案。改善诊断途径、公众意识和有针对性的研究对于控制 HMPV 感染至关重要。需要进一步的临床试验来建立安全有效的治疗方案。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 针对抗病毒药物、单克隆抗体及疫苗的持续研究对于有效疾病管理至关重要。

Further clinical trials are needed to establish safe and effective therapeutic options.
abstract_zh: 引言:人偏肺病毒(HMPV)是一种重要的呼吸道病原体,可在不同年龄段人群中引发感染,尤其是在幼儿、免疫功能低下者及老年人中。尽管其具有重要的临床意义,但目前尚无获批的抗病毒药物或针对人偏肺病毒的特异性治疗方法,亟需进一步研究治疗和预防策略。方法:通过系统性文献综述,检索同行评议期刊、临床试验及近期研究,重点关注人偏肺病毒感染。提取并分析数据,以评估抗病毒药物、单克隆抗体、免疫调节剂及疫苗候选物的有效性。结果:研究表明,人偏肺病毒主要靶向呼吸道上皮细胞,触发免疫应答,这些免疫应答既有助于病毒清除,也会导致疾病发病机制。正在研发的治疗方法,包括融合抑制剂和蛋白酶抑制剂,显示出潜力,但仍需进一步验证。免疫调节剂和中草药可能提供支持性益处,但其对人偏肺病毒的有效性尚未得到证实。疫苗研发取得进展,多个候选疫苗已进入临床前及早期临床阶段。讨论:由于人偏肺病毒的季节性流行、与其他呼吸道病毒的临床相似性以及缺乏特异性治疗方法,该病毒继续对公共卫生构成重大负担。该病毒通过多种机制逃避免疫应答,导致疾病严重程度增加,尤其是在易感人群中。尽管目前主要采用支持性治疗,但新兴的抗病毒药物和疫苗可能为未来提供解决方案。改善诊断可及性、提高公众意识及开展针对性研究对于控制人偏肺病毒感染至关重要。结论:由于缺乏针对性治疗方法和疫苗,人偏肺病毒继续对公共卫生构成挑战。针对抗病毒药物、单克隆抗体及疫苗的持续研究对于有效疾病管理至关重要。亟需进一步临床试验以确立安全有效的治疗方案。

These results can inform targeted surveillance and public health interventions for HMPV in children, particularly during seasonal surges and in specific age and gender groups.

title: Immunogenicity and Safety of the Adjuvanted Respiratory Syncytial Virus Prefusion F Protein-Based Vaccine When Co-administered With the Adjuvanted Recombinant Herpes Zoster Subunit Vaccine in Adults ≥ 50 Years of Age.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Co-administration of AS01E-adjuvanted respiratory syncytial virus vaccine (adjuvanted RSVPreF3) and AS01B-adjuvanted recombinant herpes zoster subunit vaccine (RZV), although not contraindicated, has not been previously studied in clinical trials. METHODS: This phase III, open-label, randomized (1:1) trial evaluated the immunogenicity, safety, and reactogenicity of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 when co-administered with RZV in ≥50-year-olds. The 2 vaccines were either co-administered at visit 1 (day [D] 1; Co-Ad), or were given sequentially, 1 month apart (RZV dose 1 at D1, adjuvanted RSVPreF3 at D31; Control). All participants received RZV dose-2 at D61. Non-inferiority of humoral immune responses was demonstrated if 95% confidence interval (CI) upper limits for geometric mean RSV-A/B neutralizing titers (GMT) and varicella-zoster virus anti-glycoprotein E (anti-gE) antibody concentration (GMC) ratios (Control/Co-Ad) were ≤1.5. Safety and reactogenicity were secondary endpoints. RESULTS: Overall, 530 participants (Co-Ad = 265; Control = 265) were vaccinated. Neutralizing GMT ratios for RSV-A (1.1 [95% CI = 1.0-1.4]) and RSV-B (1.0 [0.8-1.2]), and anti-gE antibody GMC ratio (1.2 [1.1-1.4]) met non-inferiority criteria. Within 7 days post-vaccination, 71.7% (Co-Ad: post-RZV dose 1 and adjuvanted RSVPreF3; grade [Gr] 3 = 3.9%), 58.5% (Control: post-RZV dose 1; Gr3 = 1.9%), and 47.8% (Control: post-adjuvanted RSVPreF3; Gr3 = 1.2%) of participants reported solicited administration-site adverse events (AEs). Post-visit 1, 73.6% (Gr3 = 9.3%) of Co-Ad and 60.4% (Gr3 = 6.2%) of control participants reported solicited systemic AEs. Within 30 days post-any vaccination, 23.4% (Gr3 = 0.8%) of Co-Ad and 30.2% (Gr3 = 1.1%) of control participants reported unsolicited AEs. No fatal or related serious AEs were reported. CONCLUSIONS: Immunogenicity, reactogenicity, and safety data support the co-administration of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 and RZV. CLINICAL TRIALS REGISTRATION: NCT05966090.
journal: Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America

title: Immunogenicity and Safety of Co-administration of Adjuvanted Respiratory Syncytial Virus Prefusion F Protein Vaccine With 20-Valent Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine in Adults Aged ≥60 Years: A Randomized, Non-inferiority Trial.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) illness and pneumococcal disease present high disease burden and health risks to older adults. Vaccination against these 2 illnesses is a key strategy to reduce this burden, and co-administration of the 2 vaccines could enhance vaccine uptake. This study evaluated the immunogenicity, safety, and reactogenicity of co-administration of adjuvanted RSV prefusion F protein vaccine (adjuvanted RSVPreF3) with 20-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV20) in adults aged ≥60 years. METHODS: This phase III, open-label, randomized, non-inferiority trial was conducted across 38 centers in Belgium, Poland, Spain, and the United States. Participants (N = 1112) were randomized 1:1 to receive adjuvanted RSVPreF3 vaccine and PCV20 vaccine either concomitantly (Co-Ad group) or 1 month apart (Control group). The primary objectives were to assess immunogenicity as measured by RSV-A and RSV-B neutralizing titers and opsonophagocytic titers for the PCV20 serotypes. Safety and reactogenicity were assessed as secondary objectives. RESULTS: All primary immunogenicity objectives were met. The upper limit of the 95% confidence interval of the geometric mean titer ratios for RSV-A, RSV-B, and all 20 PCV20 serotypes was within the pre-defined non-inferiority margins. Safety profiles were similar across both groups, with most adverse events being mild to moderate in severity and of short duration. Serious adverse events and potential immune-mediated diseases were rare and unrelated to vaccination. CONCLUSIONS: Co-administration of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 vaccine and PCV20 vaccine in older adults is immunologically non-inferior to their sequential administration, with an acceptable safety profile. These findings support co-administration as a strategy to enhance vaccine uptake. CLINICAL TRIALS REGISTRATION: NCT05879107.
journal: Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America

title: Phase 2a Randomized Placebo-Controlled Human Challenge Trial of the Respiratory Syncytial Virus L-Protein Inhibitor S-337395 for Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection.
abstract: BACKGROUND: S-337395 is a novel inhibitor of the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) L-protein, and a potential oral antiviral against RSV. This phase 2a, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, single-center, proof-of-concept trial conducted in the United Kingdom (April-October 2024) evaluated the efficacy, safety, and dose-response relationship of S-337395 against RSV infection in a human challenge model. METHODS: Healthy adults aged 18-55 years meeting predefined eligibility criteria were inoculated with RSV-A Memphis 37b on Day 0. Nasal washes were collected for quantitative reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) assessment twice daily on Days 2-12 and once on Day 13. Participants were randomized 5:13:13:13:13 to receive S-337395 (1, 10, 30, or 300 mg) or placebo, once daily for 5 days upon evidence of infection. Efficacy analyses were conducted in participants with confirmed RSV infection in intent-to-treat infected (ITT-I) set. Safety was assessed in all randomized participants. Dose-response was evaluated across a wide dose range (1-300 mg). RESULTS: Of 114 randomized participants, 60 comprised the ITT-I set. Covariate-adjusted mean viral load area under the curve (VL-AUC) was significantly lower in the 30- and 300-mg groups by qRT-PCR (64.87% and 88.94% reductions, respectively, both P < .05) and by viral culture assay (72.32% and 86.17% reductions, respectively, both P < .05). Total symptom score AUC was 78.15% lower in the 300-mg group (P < .05). S-337395 was well-tolerated without any safety concerns. CONCLUSIONS: S-337395 significantly reduced viral load, viral titer, and symptoms, and was well-tolerated in this human challenge study. Clinical Trial Registration: ISRCTN24865912.

title: Multimodal reasoning for broadly neutralizing antibody discovery from label-free human B cell repertoires across virus families
abstract: Discovering broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) from human natural immune repertoires remains a fundamental challenge in immunology, hindered by: the extreme rarity of bnAb, incomplete understanding of their cellular origins across pathogens, and the inability of existing computational tools to generalize across emerging viral threats. Here we present ImmuneAgent, a closed-loop AI system that integrates multimodal reasoning with continual meta-learning and wet-lab feedback to overcome these barriers. Applied to screen the natural BCR repertoires from vaccinated or infected cohorts, the system achieves a ~55% neutralization antibody discovery rate (60 of 110 cloned candidates) and a ~11% bnAb yield (12 of 110), substantially outperforming a state-of-the-art sequence-based neutralization predictor or cofolding models evaluated at the same cloning budget. Five ImmuneAgent-discovered antibodies conferred 100% in vivo protection against lethal influenza challenge, comparable to the clinical-stage therapeutic MEDI8852. The system recovered the cellular and structural determinants of bnAb activity and identified FCRL5+CD27+ atypical memory B cells as a conserved bnAb reservoir and hydrophobic interface enrichment as a cross-viral structural signature, which generalized to unseen antigens, discovering human metapneumovirus (hMPV) cross-neutralizing and human papillomavirus (HPV)-neutralizing antibodies without antigen-specific sorting. These results validate that ImmuneAgent is a generalizable framework for rapid therapeutic antibody discovery against emerging viral threats.

Here we present ImmuneAgent, a closed-loop AI system that integrates multimodal reasoning with continual meta-learning and wet-lab feedback to overcome these barriers. Applied to screen the natural BCR repertoires from vaccinated or infected cohorts, the system achieves a ~55% neutralization antibody discovery rate (60 of 110 cloned candidates) and a ~11% bnAb yield (12 of 110), substantially outperforming a state-of-the-art sequence-based neutralization predictor or cofolding models evaluated at the same cloning budget. Five ImmuneAgent-discovered antibodies conferred 100% in vivo protection against lethal influenza challenge, comparable to the clinical-stage therapeutic MEDI8852. The system recovered the cellular and structural determinants of bnAb activity and identified FCRL5+CD27+ atypical memory B cells as a conserved bnAb reservoir and hydrophobic interface enrichment as a cross-viral structural signature, which generalized to unseen antigens, discovering human metapneumovirus (hMPV) cross-neutralizing and human papillomavirus (HPV)-neutralizing antibodies without antigen-specific sorting. These results validate that ImmuneAgent is a generalizable framework for rapid therapeutic antibody discovery against emerging viral threats.

abstract_zh: 从人类自然免疫库中发现广泛中和抗体 (bnAb) 仍然是免疫学中的一项基本挑战,其阻碍因素包括:bnAb 极其稀有、对病原体细胞起源的不完全了解以及现有计算工具无法概括新兴病毒威胁。在这里,我们展示了 ImmuneAgent,这是一个闭环人工智能系统,它将多模态推理与持续元学习和湿实验室反馈相结合,以克服这些障碍。该系统应用于从接种疫苗或感染的 队列研究 中筛选天然 BCR 库,实现了约 55% 的中和抗体发现率(110 个克隆候选者中的 60 个)和约 11% bnAb 产量(110 个克隆候选者中的 12 个),大大优于在相同克隆预算下评估的最先进的基于序列的中和预测器或共折叠模型。ImmuneAgent 发现的五种抗体可针对致命流感攻击提供 100% 体内保护,与临床阶段治疗药物 MEDI8852 相当。该系统恢复了 bnAb 活性的细胞和结构决定因素,并将 FCRL5+CD27+ 非典型记忆 B 细胞鉴定为保守的 bnAb 储存宿主,并将疏水界面富集鉴定为交叉病毒结构特征,其推广到看不见的抗原,发现 人偏肺病毒 (hMPV) 交叉中和和人乳头瘤病毒 (HPV) 中和抗体,无需抗原特异性分选。这些结果验证了 ImmuneAgent 是一个通用框架,可用于快速发现新出现的病毒威胁的治疗性抗体。

title: The Effectiveness of Nirsevimab on Antibiotic Use in Children Using Target Trial Emulation.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Nirsevimab is a monoclonal antibody with demonstrated efficacy in preventing respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections in infants. Because acute respiratory tract infections (ARTIs), including viral infections, often lead to antibiotic prescribing, we aimed to determine the effectiveness of nirsevimab on antibiotic prescribing among infants with medically attended ARTIs. METHODS: A primary care attendee cohort was established using electronic health record data from 32 diverse practices across a healthcare network to emulate a target trial comparing nirsevimab to no treatment among infants <8 months. Eligible infants were seen at a primary care practice within 14 days of life. Primary outcomes included time to first antibiotic prescription for (1) outpatient ARTIs, (2) outpatient encounters for bronchiolitis, and (3) RSV-related hospitalizations. Nirsevimab effectiveness was calculated as 1 minus the risk ratio for each primary outcome. RESULTS: Among 15 341 patients who met inclusion criteria, 7413 received nirsevimab. Compared with no treatment, nirsevimab administration led to a 14.4% (95% CI: 7.8%, 20.6%) reduction in antibiotic prescribing for outpatient ARTIs, a 40.3% (95% CI: 25.1%, 52.5%) reduction in antibiotic prescribing for outpatient bronchiolitis, and a 69.4% (95% CI: 4.8%, 90.1%) reduction in antibiotic prescribing for RSV-related hospitalizations. CONCLUSIONS: Nirsevimab administration in primary care reduced antibiotic use for ARTIs in both ambulatory and inpatient settings.

full_text: AbstractBackgroundThe detection of Aspergillus in the lower respiratory tract complicates the clinical course of viral pneumonia and is linked to poor outcomes, but prior evidence is confined to the intensive care unit (ICU) or single-virus settings (e.g., influenza or SARS-CoV-2). Whether its frequency and prognostic significance differ across viral etiologies in hospitalized adults remains unknown.MethodsThis multicenter retrospective cohort study included adults with community-acquired viral pneumonia at seven tertiary hospitals in China (2017-2025). Patients were categorized into SARS-CoV-2, influenza, or other viral groups. The exposure was lower respiratory tract Aspergillus detection (via using culture, real-time PCR, or metagenomic next-generation sequencing). The primary outcome was in-hospital all-cause mortality.ResultsAmong 929 patients, Aspergillus was detected in 175 (18.8%). The detection rates differed significantly across viral etiologies (33.2% in patients with influenza, 14.6% in those with SARS-CoV-2, and 7.4% in those with other viruses; P < 0.001). In the fully adjusted model, Aspergillus detection was independently associated with increased overall mortality (aOR = 2.99; 95% CI 1.60–5.58; P < 0.001), but the association varied markedly by viral etiology. Virus-stratified analyses revealed that in influenza, Aspergillus detection remained independently associated with mortality after multivariable adjustment, and the association was consistently observed across prespecified subgroups, including non-ventilated patients, whereas in SARS-CoV-2, the association was largely confined to ventilated patients.ConclusionLower respiratory tract Aspergillus detection differed substantially by viral etiology and was most frequent in patients with influenza pneumonia. It was independently associated with increased mortality across all influenza subgroups, including non-ventilated patients, whereas in SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia this association was largely confined to mechanical ventilation patients. These findings support a virus-stratified approach to fungal surveillance and warrant prospective validation.Keywords: Aspergillus, cohort study, influenza, mortality, SARS-CoV-2, viral pneumonia 2.Materials and methods2.1.Ethics approvalThe study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Shijiazhuang People’s Hospital (Approval No. 2026090) and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Given the retrospective design and use of anonymized data, the Ethics Committee waived the requirement for informed consent.2.2.Study participantsWe included patients admitted to seven tertiary hospitals in China with viral pneumonia between February 1, 2017, and April 1, 2025, reported as per STROBE guidelines (von Elm et al., 2007).Inclusion criteria: (1) diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia using standard criteria (clinical signs and symptoms plus radiographic evidence of alveolar inflammation, per the 2025 ATS guideline (Jones et al., 2026); (2) laboratory confirmation of viral infection. This confirmation required either a positive result for viral pathogens (including SARS-CoV-2, influenza A/B, adenovirus, herpes simplex virus, rhinovirus, parainfluenza, human coronavirus, respiratory syncytial virus, cytomegalovirus, coxsackievirus, human metapneumovirus, and varicella-zoster virus) via real-time PCR or metagenomic next-generation sequencing of respiratory specimens (sputum, tracheal aspirates, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, or nasopharyngeal swabs), or a positive rapid antigen test for SARS-CoV-2 or influenza.Patients were excluded if they met any of the following criteria: hospitalization within 30 days prior to admission; pulmonary fungal infection within 3 months prior to admission; pulmonary embolism; NYHA class III-IV heart failure; active tuberculosis or nontuberculous mycobacterial infection; HIV infection; pregnancy or lactation; or mixed viral infection.2.3.Data collectionClinical data were systematically extracted from the electronic medical records of all seven participating centers and entered into a standardized case report form via the Free Electronic Data Capture system (version 2.0; Beijing Free Clinical Medical Technology Co., Ltd., Beijing, China). Data extraction was performed independently by two trained clinical research coordinators at each site. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion or by adjudication from the principal investigator.The following data domains were collected for each patient: (1) Demographic and baseline characteristics, including age, sex, and smoking history; (2) Comorbidities, including: hypertension, diabetes mellitus, coronary heart disease (CHD), cerebrovascular disease, chronic lung disease (asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or diffuse interstitial lung disease), chronic kidney disease (CKD) (with or without dialysis), chronic liver disease (hepatitis, cirrhosis, or liver failure), and immunosuppression (attributable to underlying autoimmune disease, long-term immunosuppressive medication, or active malignancy); (3) Vital signs at hospital admission, including: maximum body temperature (Tmax), pulse rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and respiratory rate; (4) Laboratory parameters obtained within 24 h of admission, including: complete blood count [white blood cell (WBC) count, neutrophil (NEU) count, lymphocyte (LYM) count, monocyte count, hemoglobin (HGB), and platelet (PLT) count], liver function tests (alanine aminotransferase; aspartate aminotransferase and lactate dehydrogenase), creatine kinase, serum albumin (ALB), serum creatinine, prothrombin time, D-dimer, C-reactive protein (CRP), and procalcitonin (PCT); and arterial blood gas analysis (pH, arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide, arterial partial pressure of oxygen, oxygenation index [arterial partial pressure of oxygen/fraction of inspired oxygen], and lactic acid (Lac)]; (5) Microbiological data, specifically: the results of Aspergillus detection in lower respiratory tract samples (sputum, tracheal aspirate, or bronchoalveolar lavage fluid) via fungal culture, real-time PCR, or metagenomic next-generation sequencing. Sputum specimens were subjected to cytological quality screening prior to processing; eligibility was defined as fewer than 10 squamous epithelial cells and more than 25 leukocytes per low-power field. (6) Treatment data, including antiviral, antibacterial, and antifungal therapies, systemic glucocorticoid use, and invasive mechanical ventilation; and (7) clinical outcomes, specifically in-hospital all-cause mortality, and 28-day in-hospital mortality was also assessed as a secondary outcome.2.4.Statistical analysisStatistical analyses were performed using R version 3.6.3 and Free Statistics version 2.2. Missing laboratory and clinical values (e.g., D-dimer, albumin) were imputed using multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE; 20 imputed datasets); the proportions of missing data are summarized in Supplementary Table S1. Continuous variables are presented as means ± standard deviations (SD) or medians with interquartile ranges (IQR), and were compared using analysis of variance (ANOVA) or the Kruskal-Wallis test, as appropriate. Categorical variables are expressed as frequencies (percentages) and were compared using the Pearson χ2 or Fisher’s exact test. Univariate logistic regression models were used to estimate odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for Aspergillus detection and in-hospital mortality. Variables with P < 0.05 in the univariate analysis, alongside clinically relevant confounders, were incorporated into sequentially built multivariable models: Model 1 adjusted for demographics (age, sex, and smoking status); Model 2 further adjusted for inflammatory markers and laboratory findings; Model 3 additionally included comorbidities; and Model 4 (the full model) further incorporated antiviral and antibacterial therapies, systemic glucocorticoids, as well as mechanical ventilation. Pre-specified stratified analyses were performed to assess effect modification by age (<60 vs. ≥60 years), sex, presence of comorbidities, and mechanical ventilation in the overall cohort. In addition, we conducted subgroup analyses within the influenza and SARS-CoV-2 subgroups to assess the moderating effects of age, sex, and mechanical ventilation on the effect. Interactions were assessed by including multiplicative interaction terms in the logistic regression models, and statistical significance was determined by likelihood ratio tests. A two-sided P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Patients in the SARS-CoV-2 group were the oldest (75.6 ± 11.5 years), and had the longest hospital stay (25.5 ± 9.9 days). This group also exhibited the highest prevalences of hypertension, CHD, and cerebrovascular disease, alongside the lowest ALB and LYM counts, and the highest rate of glucocorticoid use (66.3%). Conversely, chronic lung disease was most common in the influenza group (29.6%), which also demonstrated the highest D-dimer levels and the highest frequencies of antiviral (75.2%) and antifungal (36.0%) therapies. Meanwhile, a history of smoking was most prevalent among patients infected with other viruses (45.3%).Table 1Baseline clinical characteristics, treatments, and outcomes of patients stratified by viral Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion or by adjudication from the principal investigator.The following data domains were collected for each patient: (1) Demographic and baseline characteristics, including age, sex, and smoking history; (2) Comorbidities, including: hypertension, diabetes mellitus, coronary heart disease (CHD), cerebrovascular disease, chronic lung disease (asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or diffuse interstitial lung disease), chronic kidney disease (CKD) (with or without dialysis), chronic liver disease (hepatitis, cirrhosis, or liver failure), and immunosuppression (attributable to underlying autoimmune disease, long-term immunosuppressive medication, or active malignancy); (3) Vital signs at hospital admission, including: maximum body temperature (Tmax), pulse rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and respiratory rate; (4) Laboratory parameters obtained within 24 h of admission, including: complete blood count [white blood cell (WBC) count, neutrophil (NEU) count, lymphocyte (LYM) count, monocyte count, hemoglobin (HGB), and platelet (PLT) count], liver function tests (alanine aminotransferase; aspartate aminotransferase and lactate dehydrogenase), creatine kinase, serum albumin (ALB), serum creatinine, prothrombin time, D-dimer, C-reactive protein (CRP), and procalcitonin (PCT); and arterial blood gas analysis (pH, arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide, arterial partial pressure of oxygen, oxygenation index [arterial partial pressure of oxygen/fraction of inspired oxygen], and lactic acid (Lac)]; (5) Microbiological data, specifically: the results of Aspergillus detection in lower respiratory tract samples (sputum, tracheal aspirate, or bronchoalveolar lavage fluid) via fungal culture, real-time PCR, or metagenomic next-generation sequencing. Sputum specimens were subjected to cytological quality screening prior to processing; eligibility was defined as fewer than 10 squamous epithelial cells and more than 25 leukocytes per low-power field. (6) Treatment data, including antiviral, antibacterial, and antifungal therapies, systemic glucocorticoid use, and invasive mechanical ventilation; and (7) clinical outcomes, specifically in-hospital all-cause mortality, and 28-day in-hospital mortality was also assessed as a secondary outcome.2.4.Statistical analysisStatistical analyses were performed using R version 3.6.3 and Free Statistics version 2.2. Missing laboratory and clinical values (e.g., D-dimer, albumin) were imputed using multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE; 20 imputed datasets); the proportions of missing data are summarized in Supplementary Table S1. Continuous variables are presented as means ± standard deviations (SD) or medians with interquartile ranges (IQR), and were compared using analysis of variance (ANOVA) or the Kruskal-Wallis test, as appropriate. Categorical variables are expressed as frequencies (percentages) and were compared using the Pearson χ2 or Fisher’s exact test. Univariate logistic regression models were used to estimate odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for Aspergillus detection and in-hospital mortality. Variables with P < 0.05 in the univariate analysis, alongside clinically relevant confounders, were incorporated into sequentially built multivariable models: Model 1 adjusted for demographics (age, sex, and smoking status); Model 2 further adjusted for inflammatory markers and laboratory findings; Model 3 additionally included comorbidities; and Model 4 (the full model) further incorporated antiviral and antibacterial therapies, systemic glucocorticoids, as well as mechanical ventilation. Pre-specified stratified analyses were performed to assess effect modification by age (<60 vs. ≥60 years), sex, presence of comorbidities, and mechanical ventilation in the overall cohort. In addition, we conducted subgroup analyses within the influenza and SARS-CoV-2 subgroups to assess the moderating effects of age, sex, and mechanical ventilation on the effect. Interactions were assessed by including multiplicative interaction terms in the logistic regression models, and statistical significance was determined by likelihood ratio tests. A two-sided P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionIn this multicenter cohort of 929 hospitalized patients with viral pneumonia, Aspergillus detection in the lower respiratory tract differed significantly by viral etiology, being highest in influenza (33.2%), intermediate in SARS-CoV-2 (14.6%), and lowest in other viral pneumonias (7.4%). Aspergillus detection was independently associated with a substantially increased risk of all-cause mortality, although this association varied by virus type and was most pronounced in influenza. Subgroup analysis further indicated that, in influenza pneumonia, this association remained robust across different genders, age groups, and ventilatory statuses; whereas in SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia, the impact of Aspergillus detection on prognosis was primarily observed in male patients, elderly patients, and those requiring mechanical ventilation, with ventilatory status showing a significant interaction (interaction P-value < 0.001).Reported rates of viral pneumonia-associated Aspergillus vary widely across studies, reflecting differences in setting, case definitions, and diagnostic sensitivity rather than a single true prevalence. The pooled prevalence of IAPA in ICU patients is approximately 19.2% (range 6.4%–62.2%) (Lu et al., 2024). Similarly, the pooled prevalence of CAPA is highly heterogeneous, reported at 11.1% in ICU observational studies (Feys et al., 2021) and 17.5% in a subsequent meta-analysis (range, 2.5%–47.2%) (Gioia et al., 2024). Importantly, the burden is not confined to the ICU. CAPA has been reported in 15.7% of sub-ICU patients (Iacovelli et al., 2024) and 3.8% of inpatients during the Omicron wave (associated with a 43.5% mortality rate) (Wang et al., 2024). Furthermore, pulmonary aspergillosis occurs in 5%–33% of selected immunocompromised cohorts following other non-influenza viral infections (e.g., RSV, parainfluenza, and adenovirus) (Apostolopoulou et al., 2021).Unlike previous studies that confined their cohorts to ICU patients or those meeting strict ECMM/ISHAM consensus criteria (Verweij et al., 2020; Koehler et al., 2021), we enrolled a broader spectrum of hospitalized adults. As a result, our endpoint captures clinically meaningful airway carriage, rather than focusing solely on adjudicated IPA. To our knowledge, no prior study has compared lower respiratory tract Aspergillus detection across influenza, SARS-CoV-2, and other viral pneumonias within a single cohort. Previously, the largest comparative study was confined to intubated ICU patients (Rouzé et al., 2022), while another prospective study was limited to 140 critically ill patients (Ali et al., 2022). Furthermore, other analyses examined non-influenza viruses exclusively in highly selected transplant or hematologic populations (Magira et al., 2019; Apostolopoulou et al., 2021). Therefore, this analysis provides the first integrated, virus-stratified estimate of Aspergillus positivity and its prognostic significance across the full severity spectrum of routine inpatient care.The stepwise gradient in detection likely reflects virus-specific remodeling of pulmonary antifungal immunity rather than differential environmental exposure. Influenza induces a multi-level collapse of antifungal defense that includes epithelial barrier disruption, alveolar macrophage depletion, impaired phagocytic killing, and IFN-γ-driven suppression of the Th17/IL-22 axis (Short et al., 2016; Salazar et al., 2022; Feys et al., 2024; Seldeslachts et al., 2024). In a co-infection model, genetic ablation of IFN-γ restored Th17 responses and antifungal activity, identifying IFN-γ as a promising therapeutic target (Seldeslachts et al., 2024). In contrast, SARS-CoV-2 primarily causes pulmonary endotheliitis and microthrombosis (Ackermann et al., 2020; Bonaventura et al., 2021); furthermore, the associated hyperinflammation frequently requires corticosteroid therapy, thereby driving iatrogenic immunosuppression (Horby et al., 2021; Salazar et al., 2022; Shah et al., 2023; Xiang et al., 2025). Because cytokine-mediated inflammation and microvascular thrombosis are themselves dominant lethal factors in COVID-19, the independent prognostic impact of Aspergillus is statistically diluted by stronger mortality drivers. In our cohort, 66.3% of SARS-CoV-2 patients received glucocorticoids, compared to 23.6% of influenza patients; notably, corticosteroid exposure beyond 10 days has been linked to higher CAPA risk (OR 3.17; 95% CI 1.02–9.83) and increased mortality (77.1% vs. 43.2%, P < 0.0001) (Shah et al., 2023). These factors explain why, after adjusting for glucocorticoid use and mechanical ventilation, the prognostic significance of Aspergillus detection in SARS-CoV-2 patients was no longer evident (Model 4: aOR = 2.07; 95% CI 0.77–5.55; P = 0.15), and that detection of Aspergillus was not associated with increased mortality in SARS-CoV-2 patients not receiving mechanical ventilation (OR = 0.54, P = 0.316), suggesting that in milder cases, a positive fungal test result may represent colonization or a secondary finding rather than a lethal factor. In contrast, among mechanically ventilated patients, the 100% mortality rate in the Aspergillus-positive group highlighted the exceptionally poor outcomes observed in mechanically ventilated patients with severe COVID-19 and Aspergillus detection. However, the small sample size precluded precise risk assessment. These findings suggest that Aspergillus detection in COVID-19 patients primarily reflects the intensity of treatment and disease severity, rather than a direct cause of death. In infections caused by other viruses (e.g., rhinovirus, RSV) (Sajjan et al., 2008; Pickles and DeVincenzo, 2015; Horton et al., 2025), anatomically restricted airway injury, combined with younger age, lower comorbidity burden, and lower glucocorticoid exposure (16.8%), likely preserves immune reserve, thereby limiting both Aspergillus detection and its prognostic impact.In viral-associated pulmonary aspergillosis, distinguishing colonization from invasive disease is challenging, as galactomannan testing and culture cannot reliably differentiate them in critically ill patients (Donnelly et al., 2019; Verweij et al., 2020). In a study utilizing histopathological validation, tissue invasion was confirmed in 55% of probable IAPA cases and 50% of probable CAPA cases, including one case without antemortem clinical suspicion (Vanderbeke et al., 2023). Others have argued that microbiological detection of Aspergillus in severe viral pneumonia often reflects true infection, supporting preemptive antifungal therapy in high-risk patients (Albrich and Lamoth, 2023). Our data extend these observations beyond the ICU. In this multicenter cohort encompassing multiple viral etiologies and a full spectrum of disease severity, the detection of Aspergillus in the lower respiratory tract was a strong and independent prognostic factor for mortality in influenza patients (fully aOR = 13.77; 95% CI 2.75–68.88) but not in those with other viral pneumonias. This is consistent with the rapid clinical course described for IAPA, with a median interval of only 3 days from ICU admission to diagnosis (Schauwvlieghe et al., 2018). Our subgroup analysis further corroborated this observation. Among mechanically ventilated influenza patients with Aspergillus detection, mortality reached 90.5%. This rate approaches the 90-day mortality reported for invasive tracheobronchial aspergillosis (Nyga et al., 2020). In contrast, mortality among ventilated patients without Aspergillus detection was 44.0%. These findings further validate this high-risk phenotype.By evaluating lower respiratory tract Aspergillus detection across three viral groups under a unified framework, our study identifies “influenza plus lower respiratory tract Aspergillus detection” as a distinct, high-risk phenotype with an independent mortality risk several-fold higher than that of other groups. These findings challenge a uniform, one-size-fits-all approach…
full_text_sections.conclusion: 5.ConclusionsIn this multicenter cohort, lower respiratory tract Aspergillus detection rates differed significantly by viral etiology, being highest in influenza, intermediate in SARS-CoV-2, and lowest in other viral pneumonias. Its prognostic significance also varied by viral etiology. Aspergillus detection was independently associated with in-hospital mortality in influenza pneumonia. In SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia, however, this association was attenuated after full adjustment and was primarily observed among mechanically ventilated patients. These findings support further evaluation of a virus-stratified approach to fungal surveillance and warrant prospective validation.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionViral pneumonia is a major cause of hospitalization, acute respiratory failure, and mortality in adults, particularly among older adults and those with chronic comorbidities (Jain et al., 2015; Hanage and Schaffner, 2025). Moreover, high-dose or prolonged glucocorticoid use, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and mechanical ventilation are recognized risk factors for IPA (Montrucchio et al., 2021; Hurt et al., 2023; Terrones-Campos et al., 2026). analysis.summary_en: This retrospective multicenter cohort study from China investigated the association between Aspergillus detection in the lower respiratory tract and mortality in patients with viral pneumonias. The study included 929 hospitalized patients with different viral etiologies, such as influenza, SARS-CoV-2, and other viruses. Aspergillus was detected in 18.8% of patients, with the highest rate in the influenza group (33.2%) and the lowest in other viruses (7.4%). In-hospital mortality was significantly higher in the SARS-CoV-2 and influenza groups compared to other virus groups. The study found that Aspergillus detection was independently associated with increased mortality, but the association varied by viral etiology, with influenza showing the strongest link. These findings highlight the importance of monitoring for Aspergillus in patients with viral pneumonia, particularly influenza, for risk assessment and clinical management. However, the study's retrospective design and potential confounding factors limit the confidence in the results.

full_text: BackgroundCOVID-19-related non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) disrupted the circulation of many respiratory pathogens. After these measures were lifted, pediatric respiratory pathogen activity may have changed in pathogen-specific ways. However, laboratory-based evidence using continuous multi-year data, interrupted time-series analysis, and contextual factors such as meteorology, air quality, and school calendars remains limited.MethodsWe conducted a single-center retrospective laboratory study of pediatric and neonatal inpatients aged 0–14 years with clinically diagnosed lower respiratory tract infection from January 2021 to December 2025. After 7-day deduplication within the same child, 20,250 throat-swab testing records were included. The NPI period was January 2021–December 2022, and the post-NPI period was January 2023–December 2025. Thirteen pathogen categories were analyzed using period comparisons, interrupted time-series models, and multivariable logistic regression incorporating meteorological factors, air quality index, and school-term status.ResultsOverall positivity was higher in the post-NPI period than in the NPI period (75.4% vs. 58.8%), and co-detection was also higher in the post-NPI period (15.2% vs. 6.0%). Pathogen-specific interrupted time-series analysis showed heterogeneous patterns: human adenovirus showed a robust immediate level decrease (−13.00 percentage points; 95% CI, −20.13 to −5.87; FDR-adjusted P = 0.005), whereas human rhinovirus showed a significant positive trend change after the January 2023 interruption (+1.07 percentage points per month; 95% CI, 0.63–1.50; FDR-adjusted P < 0.001), with a positive post-NPI slope (+0.64 percentage points per month). Higher temperature was associated with lower positivity of human respiratory syncytial virus, influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus, and influenza B virus, but higher positivity of human parainfluenza virus and human bocavirus. School-term status was associated with higher human rhinovirus positivity (aOR, 1.84; 95% CI, 1.34–2.52; FDR-adjusted P = 0.002).ConclusionThe NPI and post-NPI periods showed distinct and heterogeneous temporal patterns in pediatric respiratory pathogen detection. These findings support integrated hospital-based laboratory surveillance centered on pathogen-specific temporal trends and interpreted alongside demographic, multi-pathogen, environmental, school-calendar, and longer-term temporal context. 2Materials and methods2.1Study design, setting, and data sourceThis single-center, laboratory-based retrospective observational study was conducted in the Department of Clinical Laboratory at Beijing Anzhen Nanchong Hospital of Capital Medical University and Nanchong Central Hospital, located in Nanchong, Sichuan Province, China. The hospital is a tertiary general hospital and clinical teaching hospital that receives patients from Nanchong and surrounding areas. Pediatric respiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing records from January 1, 2021, to December 31, 2025, were extracted from the laboratory information system. Throughout the study period, the data-collecting hospital, clinical laboratory, and respiratory pathogen testing framework remained consistent. Annual pediatric and neonatal inpatient volumes from 2021 to 2025 were obtained from hospital administrative records and used to calculate the number of respiratory pathogen testing records per 100 inpatient admissions as a contextual measure of testing volume across study periods.2.2Study populationEligible testing records were from pediatric or neonatal inpatients aged 0–14 years with a clinician-recorded diagnosis of lower respiratory tract infection on the laboratory test request. These patients underwent routine 13-target multiplex respiratory pathogen testing between January 1, 2021, and December 31, 2025. Testing was ordered by clinicians according to the child's clinical presentation and diagnostic needs. Throat swabs were collected for respiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing. Records were required to contain complete information on sex, age, application date, and pathogen detection results. Outpatient and emergency department records were not included. Throughout the study period, the source wards, age range, eligibility criteria, and specimen type remained consistent.A total of 21,132 original identification records were initially available. After preliminary data cleaning, variable harmonization, and verification of key fields, 20,296 preliminary testing records were retained. To reduce the influence of repeated short-term testing from the same child, 7-day deduplication was performed using medical record numbers. For each child, testing records were ordered chronologically by application time; when multiple respiratory pathogen tests occurred within a 7-day window, only the first record was retained, whereas a test performed more than 7 days after the previously retained record was considered a new testing event. After deduplication, 46 short-term duplicate records were removed, leaving 20,250 testing records for the main analysis, including 6,490 records from the NPI period and 13,760 from the post-NPI period. The final dataset covered 60 consecutive months from January 2021 to December 2025. The overall study design, data-cleaning process, 7-day deduplication procedure, study-period classification, and analytical workflow are summarized in Figure 1.Figure 1Study design, data cleaning, and analytical workflow. The figure shows the data source, exclusion process, 7-day deduplication, study-period classification, and analytical framework. The NPI period was defined as January 2021 to December 2022, and the post-NPI period was defined as January 2023 to December 2025. During 7-day deduplication, only the first testing record from the same child within a 7-day window was retained. NPI, non-pharmaceutical intervention.Flowchart of study record selection and analysis. A total of 21,132 pediatric 13-pathogen respiratory nucleic acid testing records were screened; 836 records were excluded during data cleaning, leaving 20,296 preliminary records. After excluding 46 non-first repeat tests within 7 days, 20,250 records remained. These were classified into the NPI period (January 2021-December 2022; n = 6,490) and post-NPI period (January 2023–December 2025; n = 13,760), followed by risk-ratio, interrupted time-series, multivariable, age-stratified, co-detection, and sensitivity analyses.Children were categorized into four age groups: <1, 1–<3, 3–<6, and 6–14 years. This age stratification was selected according to commonly used pediatric respiratory infection epidemiology and the social contact patterns of children in China, broadly corresponding to infancy, early childhood mainly under home care, kindergarten age, and school age.2.3Respiratory pathogen testing and pathogen definitionsRespiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing was performed using a multiplex detection kit for 13 respiratory pathogens based on fluorescence PCR followed by capillary electrophoresis (PN: 1060071; Health GeneTech Co., Ltd., Ningbo, China). Nucleic acid extraction was performed using a TANBead SLA-32 automated nucleic acid extraction system. PCR amplification was performed using a SLAN-96P real-time PCR system. Amplification products were detected using an Applied Biosystems 3500 Dx Genetic Analyzer for capillary electrophoresis-based detection and fragment analysis. Sample processing, nucleic acid extraction, PCR amplification, capillary electrophoresis, quality control, and result interpretation were performed according to the manufacturer's instructions and local standard operating procedures.The main analysis included 13 respiratory pathogen categories: influenza A virus not further classified by this panel (InfA-NFC), influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus, seasonal influenza A (H3N2) virus, influenza B virus, human respiratory syncytial virus, human parainfluenza virus, human metapneumovirus, human rhinovirus, human adenovirus, seasonal human coronaviruses, human bocavirus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Chlamydia spp. In this study, InfA-NFC referred to records positive for the manufacturer-reported generic influenza A target, listed as InfA in the manufacturer's instructions, but not classified as influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus or seasonal influenza A (H3N2) virus. The seasonal human coronaviruses category did not include SARS-CoV-2. Throughout the study period, SARS-CoV-2 testing, when clinically indicated, was performed through a separate dedicated nucleic acid testing pathway and was therefore not included in the fixed 13-target respiratory pathogen panel analyzed in this study. The Chlamydia category was not further differentiated into C. trachomatis or C. pneumoniae. Pathogen abbreviations, full pathogen names, manufacturer-reported detection targets, and limits of detection are provided in Supplementary Table S1.A composite influenza A variable was defined as positivity for any influenza A-related analytic category, including InfA-NFC, influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus, or seasonal influenza A(H3N2) virus. This composite variable was used only for descriptive summaries and was not included as an additional category in the main risk ratio, multiple-comparison, interrupted time-series, or multivariable regression analyses to avoid double counting. Overall positivity was defined as positivity for at least one of the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories. Co-detection was defined as positivity for two or more of the 13 main pathogen categories in the same testing record. Positivity and co-detection rates were calculated using the corresponding number of testing records as the denominator. A 13-target-negative record was defined as a testing record in which none of the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories was detected. Overall positivity and 13-target-negative proportions describe laboratory detection among tested pediatric and neonatal inpatients and were not intended as estimates of community incidence or prevalence.2.4Study periods, seasons, and school-term statusThe study period was divided according to the timing of COVID-19 policy adjustment in China and the monthly structure of the dataset. January 2021 to December 2022 was defined as the NPI period, and January 2023 to December 2025 was defined as the post-NPI period. In interrupted time-series analyses, January 2023 was treated as the first post-intervention month. Seasons were defined by calendar month: spring, March to May; summer, June to August; autumn, September to November; and winter, December to February. School-term status was defined at the calendar-day level according to the official local school calendar rather than by calendar month alone and assigned to each testing record based on the application date. Each testing record was classified as occurring during an in-school term or a vacation period. This variable was used as a population-level contextual indicator of periods with increased or decreased community contact networks related to kindergarten and school attendance.2.5Meteorological and air-quality dataDaily meteorological observations for Nanchong, Sichuan Province, China were obtained from RP5 (Reliable Prognosis), a publicly available weather data platform providing observational data from ground weather stations. Daily air quality index (AQI) records were obtained from the 2345 Weather historical weather database for Nanchong, a publicly accessible weather and air-quality information platform that provides city-level historical weather records with daily air-quality information (https://tianqi.2345.com/wea_history/57411.htm; accessed July 4, 2026). Before monthly aggregation, extracted AQI records were checked for completeness, date consistency, plausible value ranges, and temporal continuity. Daily temperature, relative humidity, and AQI records were aggregated into monthly means for each calendar month and linked to individual testing records by year-month. Temperature was modeled per 1 °C increase, relative humidity per 10% increase, and AQI per 10-unit increase. Meteorological and AQI variables were available for all 60 calendar months from January 2021 to December 2025 and were matched to the testing dataset by year-month.2.6Statistical analysisAll statistical analyses were based on the final analytic dataset of 20,250 testing records. Categorical variables were summarized as counts and percentages. Continuous variables were summarized as medians with interquartile ranges or means with standard deviations, as appropriate. All tests were two-sided, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. For multiple comparisons across the 13 main pathogen categories, the Benjamini–Hochberg method was used to control the false discovery rate (FDR). All statistical analyses were performed using Python software. Data management and aggregation were conducted using pandas and NumPy. Statistical calculations and modeling were performed using SciPy and statsmodels, and figures were generated using matplotlib.2.6.1Baseline characteristics and period comparisonsBaseline characteristics and pathogen detection profiles were compared between the NPI and post-NPI periods. Categorical variables were compared using the χ2 test or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate. Continuous variables were compared using the Mann–Whitney U test or t test, depending on distributional characteristics. The composite influenza A variable was presented only as a descriptive summary, with influenza A subtypes listed separately. Continuous age is presented as median (interquartile range) and was compared between the NPI and post-NPI periods using the Mann–Whitney U test.2.6.2Risk ratio analysisDetection risks for the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories were compared between the NPI and post-NPI periods. For each pathogen, positivity rates were calculated for both periods, and risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated. FDR-adjusted P values were used to assess statistical robustness under multiple testing. As an additional RSV-focused supplementary analysis, age was reclassified into clinically relevant categories for RSV burden and prevention strategies. RSV detection was first compared between children aged <2 years and those aged ≥2 years. Children were further categorized as 0–<6 months, 6–<12 months, 12–<24 months, and ≥24 months. For each category, RSV positivity was summarized for the NPI and post-NPI periods, and post-NPI vs. NPI risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), P values, and FDR-adjusted P values were calculated. This RSV-specific supplementary analysis was designed to provide clinical and public-health detail for the age windows most relevant to infant and toddler RSV prevention.2.6.3Interrupted time-series analysisTo evaluate whether the period difference in overall positivity could reflect a general long-term trend, monthly overall positivity was first analyzed using a single time-trend model without an interruption term. A segmented interrupted time-series model was then fitted using January 2023 as the first post-interruption month, corresponding to the January 8, 2023 policy transition, to estimate the pre-interruption trend, immediate level change, and post-interruption trend change. A joint Wald test evaluated the combined evidence for the immediate level and trend changes, and a grouped binomial model based on monthly positive and negative counts was used as a sensitivity analysis.Interrupted time-series (ITS) segmented regression models were used to assess immediate level changes and post-intervention trend changes in monthly pathogen positivity after the lifting of NPIs. ITS and segmented regression models are commonly used to evaluate level and slope changes after public health policy or intervention changes (21–24).For each pathogen, the monthly positivity rate was used as the outcome. The core independent variables included time, intervention status, and time after intervention. Month fixed effects were included to account for seasonality. Models were weighted by the monthly number of testing records. Newey–West robust standard errors were used to account for potential autocorrelation (25). The primary model used Newey–West lag = 1, and lag = 3 was used as a sensitivity analysis.The model was specified as: Yt = β0 + β1 × time + β2 × intervention + β3 × post-intervention time + month fixed effects + εt, where β1 represents the pre-intervention monthly trend, β2 represents the immediate level change after the lifting of NPIs, and β3 represents the post-intervention trend change.2.6.4Multivariable logistic regressionTo evaluate factors associated with pathogen positivity, separate multivariable logistic regression models were fitted for each of the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories. The core independent variables were monthly mean temperature, monthly mean relative humidity, monthly mean AQI, and school-term status. Models were adjusted for age group, sex, and pandemic phase. Because meteorological exposures, seasonality, and time trends may be correlated, season was not included in the primary model to reduce potential collinearity; this approach was consistent with general considerations in environmental time-series modeling (26). Cluster-robust standard errors were estimated at the year-month level. Results were reported as adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% CIs. To assess whether environmental and temporal associations differed between the NPI and post-NPI periods, separate interaction models were fitted by adding temperature × phase, relative humidity × phase, AQI × phase, and school term × phase terms to the pathogen-specific multivariable models. Across 13 pathogen categories and four contextual factors, 52 interaction tests were prespecified. full_text_sections.abstract: BackgroundCOVID-19-related non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) disrupted the circulation of many respiratory pathogens. After these measures were lifted, pediatric respiratory pathogen activity may have changed in pathogen-specific ways. However, laboratory-based evidence using continuous multi-year data, interrupted time-series analysis, and contextual factors such as meteorology, air quality, and school calendars remains limited.MethodsWe conducted a single-center retrospective laboratory study of pediatric and neonatal inpatients aged 0–14 years with clinically diagnosed lower respiratory tract infection from January 2021 to December 2025. After 7-day deduplication within the same child, 20,250 throat-swab testing records were included. The NPI period was January 2021–December 2022, and the post-NPI period was January 2023–December 2025. Thirteen pathogen categories were analyzed using period comparisons, interrupted time-series models, and multivariable logistic regression incorporating meteorological factors, air quality index, and school-term status.ResultsOverall positivity was higher in the post-NPI period than in the NPI period (75.4% vs. 58.8%), and co-detection was also higher in the post-NPI period (15.2% vs. 6.0%). Pathogen-specific interrupted time-series analysis showed heterogeneous patterns: human adenovirus showed a robust immediate level decrease (−13.00 percentage points; 95% CI, −20.13 to −5.87; FDR-adjusted P = 0.005), whereas human rhinovirus showed a significant positive trend change after the January 2023 interruption (+1.07 percentage points per month; 95% CI, 0.63–1.50; FDR-adjusted P < 0.001), with a positive post-NPI slope (+0.64 percentage points per month). Higher temperature was associated with lower positivity of human respiratory syncytial virus, influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus, and influenza B virus, but higher positivity of human parainfluenza virus and human bocavirus. School-term status was associated with higher human rhinovirus positivity (aOR, 1.84; 95% CI, 1.34–2.52; FDR-adjusted P = 0.002).ConclusionThe NPI and post-NPI periods showed distinct and heterogeneous temporal patterns in pediatric respiratory pathogen detection. These findings support integrated hospital-based laboratory surveillance centered on pathogen-specific temporal trends and interpreted alongside demographic, multi-pathogen, environmental, school-calendar, and longer-term temporal context.
full_text_sections.methods: 2Materials and methods2.1Study design, setting, and data sourceThis single-center, laboratory-based retrospective observational study was conducted in the Department of Clinical Laboratory at Beijing Anzhen Nanchong Hospital of Capital Medical University and Nanchong Central Hospital, located in Nanchong, Sichuan Province, China. The hospital is a tertiary general hospital and clinical teaching hospital that receives patients from Nanchong and surrounding areas. Pediatric respiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing records from January 1, 2021, to December 31, 2025, were extracted from the laboratory information system. Throughout the study period, the data-collecting hospital, clinical laboratory, and respiratory pathogen testing framework remained consistent. Annual pediatric and neonatal inpatient volumes from 2021 to 2025 were obtained from hospital administrative records and used to calculate the number of respiratory pathogen testing records per 100 inpatient admissions as a contextual measure of testing volume across study periods.2.2Study populationEligible testing records were from pediatric or neonatal inpatients aged 0–14 years with a clinician-recorded diagnosis of lower respiratory tract infection on the laboratory test request. These patients underwent routine 13-target multiplex respiratory pathogen testing between January 1, 2021, and December 31, 2025. Testing was ordered by clinicians according to the child's clinical presentation and diagnostic needs. Throat swabs were collected for respiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing. Records were required to contain complete information on sex, age, application date, and pathogen detection results. Outpatient and emergency department records were not included. Throughout the study period, the source wards, age range, eligibility criteria, and specimen type remained consistent.A total of 21,132 original identification records were initially available. After preliminary data cleaning, variable harmonization, and verification of key fields, 20,296 preliminary testing records were retained. To reduce the influence of repeated short-term testing from the same child, 7-day deduplication was performed using medical record numbers. For each child, testing records were ordered chronologically by application time; when multiple respiratory pathogen tests occurred within a 7-day window, only the first record was retained, whereas a test performed more than 7 days after the previously retained record was considered a new testing event. After deduplication, 46 short-term duplicate records were removed, leaving 20,250 testing records for the main analysis, including 6,490 records from the NPI period and 13,760 from the post-NPI period. The median age was 2.00 years overall and in both the NPI and post-NPI periods. The overall IQR was 0.75–4.00 years, while the IQRs were 0.67–4.00 years during the NPI period and 0.75–4.00 years during the post-NPI period. The largest age group was 3–<6 years (30.2%), followed by <1 year (29.4%), 1–<3 years (25.3%), and 6–14 years (15.1%). full_text_sections.discussion: 4Discussion4.1Principal findingsThis 5-year hospital-based laboratory surveillance study identified marked changes in pediatric respiratory pathogen detection across the NPI and post-NPI periods, with distinct temporal patterns across pathogens. Overall positivity was higher in the post-NPI period than in the NPI period (75.4% vs. 58.8%), and co-detection was also more frequent (15.2% vs. 6.0%). At the aggregate level, overall positivity showed a significant long-term increasing trend over the 5-year study period, whereas segmented analysis using January 2023 as the interruption point showed no statistically significant immediate level or slope change. At the pathogen-specific level, ITS analyses revealed distinct temporal trajectories across pathogens, with human adenovirus showing a robust immediate decrease and human rhinovirus showing a significant positive trend change and a positive post-NPI slope. Associations with environmental factors and school-calendar status were likewise pathogen-specific, and phase-interaction analyses further showed that selected associations with temperature, relative humidity, and school-term status differed between the NPI and post-NPI periods. Overall, these findings demonstrate a complex temporal profile of pediatric respiratory pathogen detection characterized by a long-term aggregate trend, pathogen-specific changes, and associations with environmental and school-calendar factors.4.2Overall positivity, long-term trend, and co-detection across study periodsCOVID-19-related NPIs substantially altered the circulation of common respiratory pathogens (7–11), and subsequent studies reported renewed circulation and altered epidemiological patterns of multiple respiratory pathogens following relaxation of these measures (12–16). In our study, overall positivity was higher in the post-NPI period than in the NPI period. Further analysis of the overall temporal trend showed that overall positivity increased by an average of 0.49 percentage points per month over the 5-year study period, whereas segmented analysis with January 2023 as the interruption point did not show significant changes in the overall level or trend. These findings place the higher overall positivity observed in the post-NPI period within a broader long-term upward trend and suggest that aggregate measures may not fully capture heterogeneous temporal dynamics across individual pathogens.Co-detection also increased markedly in the post-NPI period, and this increase was supported by both the period comparison and weighted ITS analysis. This pattern may reflect greater temporal overlap in the circulation of multiple respiratory pathogens, thereby increasing the likelihood of detecting more than one pathogen in the same specimen. For hospital-based laboratory surveillance, co-detection patterns provide information beyond single-pathogen positivity and add complexity to etiological attribution and laboratory interpretation. Accordingly, considering both single-pathogen temporal trends and multi-pathogen co-detection patterns may provide a more complete characterization of pediatric respiratory pathogen activity in the post-NPI period.4.3Pathogen-specific reshaping of detection patternsA central finding of this study is that pathogen detection patterns changed heterogeneously after the lifting of NPIs. Although many pathogen categories showed higher detection risks in the post-NPI period, the magnitude, timing, and stability of changes varied across pathogens. This pattern is consistent with reports of asynchronous respiratory virus resurgence and pathogen-specific recovery after relaxation of COVID-19-related restrictions (12, 14, 30). It supports the concept that the post-NPI period may represent pathogen-specific reshaping rather than a simple synchronized return to pre-pandemic seasonality. This distinction is important because aggregate respiratory pathogen positivity may obscure divergent trajectories among individual pathogens.Human rhinovirus showed the most statistically robust trend-related finding in our ITS analysis, with a significant positive trend change after the January 2023 interruption and a positive post-NPI slope. This pattern is consistent with previous pediatric studies showing that rhinovirus activity was less suppressed by NPIs and could remain prominent or increase while several other respiratory viruses showed marked reductions or altered circulation (31–33). The positive association between school-term status and human rhinovirus positivity across age strata is also consistent with evidence that school sessions, holidays, and closures can influence respiratory infection activity in children (20, 34, 35). Thus, human rhinovirus may function as a sensitive indicator of renewed pediatric contact networks in the post-NPI period. Nevertheless, school-term status in this study was defined by calendar timing and should be interpreted as a population-level contextual indicator rather than a direct measure of individual school attendance, classroom exposure, or transmission pathway.Several pathogens, including human metapneumovirus, influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus, human respiratory syncytial virus, human parainfluenza virus, and seasonal human coronaviruses, showed immediate level increases in the primary ITS model. Similar post-restriction shifts in human metapneumovirus, influenza, and other respiratory viruses have been reported after periods of reduced circulation or relaxation of COVID-19 restrictions (13, 36, 37). However, these signals in our study were attenuated after FDR correction, indicating lower statistical robustness under multiple-comparison control. These findings are still informative because they suggest transient post-NPI increases for several pathogens, while also showing that not all apparent rebounds were statistically stable after adjustment for multiple testing. For influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus, the large period-comparison RR and wide confidence interval mainly reflected sparse detections during the NPI period, indicating a marked post-NPI increase with limited precision of the RR estimate.The RSV-focused supplementary analysis further highlights the translational relevance of age-specific surveillance, consistent with previous evidence that RSV contributes substantially to acute lower respiratory infection burden in young children and that RSV activity was altered during and after COVID-19-related restriction periods (2, 10–12). Although the primary age strata were designed to reflect childcare and schooling stages in China, reclassification into RSV prevention-relevant age windows showed that children younger than 2 years accounted for most RSV-positive records and had nearly twice the overall RSV detection risk observed in older children. The highest positivity was observed in the 6–<12-month and 12–<24-month groups, supporting the importance of infant- and toddler-focused RSV prevention and surveillance strategies.
