Pathogen-specific interrupted time-series analyses further revealed different temporal trajectories, including an immediate decrease in HADV and a significant positive trend change in HRV with a positive post-NPI slope. full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionAcute respiratory infections remain a major cause of illness among children worldwide and are associated with substantial healthcare use, hospitalization, and public health burden (1). Among specific pediatric pathogens, respiratory syncytial virus, seasonal influenza virus, human metapneumovirus, and human parainfluenza virus contribute substantially to acute lower respiratory infection burden in young children (2–5). Laboratory-based surveillance in China has also shown that pediatric and community respiratory specimens can involve diverse viral and atypical pathogens rather than a single dominant target (6). These patterns vary by age, season, geography, and social contact structure, highlighting the importance of continuous laboratory-based surveillance for understanding temporal changes in pediatric respiratory pathogen activity.During the COVID-19 pandemic, non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs), such as mask wearing, school closures, reduced mobility, physical distancing, and enhanced hygiene measures, substantially altered community respiratory virus activity beyond SARS-CoV-2 (7). Observational and pediatric hospital-based studies in China showed broad impacts of NPIs on acute respiratory infections and common childhood respiratory viruses (8, 9). Respiratory syncytial virus-specific studies also reported altered epidemiological and clinical characteristics among hospitalized children during the pandemic period (10). These changes were not uniform across pathogens or regions, suggesting that pathogen biology, population susceptibility, testing behavior, and contact patterns may have interacted to shape observed laboratory detection trends.After the relaxation or lifting of COVID-19-related NPIs, many settings reported renewed activity of pediatric respiratory pathogens, but post-NPI changes have not consistently followed a single synchronized rebound pattern. Studies have described off-season or asynchronous resurgence of influenza viruses, respiratory syncytial virus, human metapneumovirus, and other common respiratory viruses after periods of reduced activity (11–13). Post-NPI resurgence or shifting epidemic features of Mycoplasma pneumoniae have also been reported in China and related pediatric studies (14, 15). The concept of immune debt has further been proposed to help explain heterogeneous pediatric respiratory infection activity after the pandemic (16). These observations suggest that the post-NPI period may be better understood as a phase of pathogen-specific reshaping of respiratory pathogen detection patterns rather than a simple return to pre-pandemic seasonality.In parallel with changes in population contact patterns, environmental and calendar-related factors may provide important context for respiratory pathogen activity. Temperature and meteorological conditions have been associated with viral seasonality and pathogen-specific acute respiratory infection patterns (17, 18). Air pollution has also been linked to respiratory infection susceptibility and pediatric respiratory health (19). School sessions have been associated with seasonal outbreaks of medically attended respiratory infections (20). Nevertheless, few studies have jointly evaluated meteorological conditions, air quality, and school-term status across multiple pediatric respiratory pathogen categories in the post-NPI period.Although evidence on post-NPI respiratory pathogen activity is increasing, the available literature remains constrained by several methodological limitations. Many studies have relied on short observation windows, selected-pathogen analyses, or simple before-and-after comparisons, which are insufficient to separate an abrupt post-policy level change from a sustained change in temporal slope. Continuous multi-year laboratory datasets that span both the NPI and post-NPI periods and simultaneously evaluate multiple pediatric respiratory pathogens remain scarce. Moreover, environmental conditions, air quality, and school-calendar context are rarely assessed within the same pathogen-specific analytical framework. These limitations restrict the ability of surveillance studies to determine whether post-NPI changes represent a uniform rebound or a more complex reshaping of pathogen-specific detection patterns.To address these gaps, we analyzed 20,250 pediatric throat-swab testing records collected over five consecutive years, from January 2021 to December 2025. We compared pathogen detection risks between the NPI and post-NPI periods, evaluated overall long-term and segmented temporal changes, applied pathogen-specific interrupted time-series models, and assessed associations of meteorological factors, air quality, and school-term status with pathogen-specific positivity, including potential variation in these associations across study periods. By integrating a large continuous laboratory dataset with time-series and contextual analyses, this study aimed to characterize pathogen-specific temporal patterns across the NPI and post-NPI periods and their relevance to hospital-based laboratory surveillance. 2.2Study populationEligible testing records were from pediatric or neonatal inpatients aged 0–14 years with a clinician-recorded diagnosis of lower respiratory tract infection on the laboratory test request. These patients underwent routine 13-target multiplex respiratory pathogen testing between January 1, 2021, and December 31, 2025. Testing was ordered by clinicians according to the child's clinical presentation and diagnostic needs. Throat swabs were collected for respiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing. Records were required to contain complete information on sex, age, application date, and pathogen detection results. Outpatient and emergency department records were not included. Throughout the study period, the source wards, age range, eligibility criteria, and specimen type remained consistent.A total of 21,132 original identification records were initially available. After preliminary data cleaning, variable harmonization, and verification of key fields, 20,296 preliminary testing records were retained. To reduce the influence of repeated short-term testing from the same child, 7-day deduplication was performed using medical record numbers. For each child, testing records were ordered chronologically by application time; when multiple respiratory pathogen tests occurred within a 7-day window, only the first record was retained, whereas a test performed more than 7 days after the previously retained record was considered a new testing event. After deduplication, 46 short-term duplicate records were removed, leaving 20,250 testing records for the main analysis, including 6,490 records from the NPI period and 13,760 from the post-NPI period. The final dataset covered 60 consecutive months from January 2021 to December 2025. The NPI period was defined as January 2021 to December 2022, and the post-NPI period was defined as January 2023 to December 2025. During 7-day deduplication, only the first testing record from the same child within a 7-day window was retained. title_original: Ecological reshaping of pediatric respiratory pathogen profiles after COVID-19-related non-pharmaceutical interventions were lifted: a 5-year interrupted time-series study

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate how the lifting of non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) related to COVID-19 affected the ecological patterns of pediatric respiratory pathogens, particularly focusing on the changes in their detection rates and temporal trends.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This 5-year interrupted time-series study was conducted at a tertiary general hospital and clinical teaching hospital in Nanchong, China, analyzing pediatric respiratory pathogen testing records from January 1, 2021, to December 31, 2025. The study included 20,250 throat-swab testing records after deduplication.
analysis.methods: The study used period comparisons, interrupted time-series models, and multivariable logistic regression incorporating meteorological factors, air quality index, and school-term status to analyze the data. Testing was conducted using a 13-target multiplex respiratory pathogen assay, and records were required to contain complete information on sex, age, application date, and pathogen detection results.
analysis.main_results: Overall positivity was higher in the post-NPI period than in the NPI period (75.4% vs. 58.8%), and co-detection was also higher (15.2% vs. Pathogen-specific interrupted time-series analysis showed a robust immediate level decrease in human adenovirus (−13.00 percentage points; 95% CI, −20.13 to −5.87; FDR-adjusted P = 0.005) and a significant positive trend change in human rhinovirus (+1.07 percentage points per month; 95% CI, 0.63–1.50; FDR-adjusted P < 0.001), with a positive post-NPI slope (+0.64 percentage points per month).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings demonstrate a complex temporal profile of pediatric respiratory pathogen detection, with distinct changes observed in specific pathogens following the lifting of NPIs, indicating that the impact of these interventions was heterogeneous across different respiratory viruses.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results provide insights into how the relaxation of NPIs has influenced the circulation and detection patterns of pediatric respiratory pathogens, which can inform future surveillance strategies and public health interventions targeting these viruses.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on hospital-based data, which may not represent the broader population. The evidence is moderate, as the findings are based on observational data and statistical models rather than experimental interventions.

analysis.summary_en: This 5-year interrupted time-series study analyzed pediatric respiratory pathogen testing records from a tertiary hospital in Nanchong, China, to assess the impact of lifting non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) related to COVID-19. The study found that overall positivity and co-detection rates increased in the post-NPI period compared to the NPI period. Pathogen-specific analyses revealed distinct changes, including a significant decrease in human adenovirus and a positive trend change in human rhinovirus. The findings highlight the heterogeneous effects of NPIs on respiratory pathogens and suggest that their removal has altered the ecological dynamics of these infections. However, the study's reliance on hospital-based data and observational methods limits the strength of the evidence, resulting in a moderate confidence assessment.

title: Trends in all-cause pneumonia and influenza hospitalization incidence by coding position – a study of US healthcare claims, 2014–2023
abstract: BACKGROUND: The hospitalization rate for pneumonia among adults has decreased in the U.S. since the early 2000's. The increasing prevalence of chronic conditions among adults, especially those associated with risk factors for pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, influenza and respiratory syncytial virus, may be contributing to a larger population susceptible to pneumonia. Existing estimates utilizing claims data may underestimate the true rates of disease due to how diagnostic coding fields are used to define outcomes. METHODS: A retrospective descriptive study of adult (> 18 years) ACPI inpatient hospitalizations was conducted using US healthcare claims data from 2014 to 2023. Principal ACPI hospitalizations were defined as those with a principal field code for ACPI only. Expanded principal ACPI hospitalizations were those with a principal code for ACPI or a principal code for sepsis, meningitis, COPD, empyema, and acute respiratory failure in combination with a secondary code for ACPI. Prevalence of risk factors indicative for pneumococcal pneumonia, RSV, or severe influenza vaccination were assessed. RESULTS: Principal ACPI showed the largest decline in incidence and this decline was greatest among the younger age groups compared to the older adults. In contrast, the expanded principal definition of ACPI captured between 48.5 and 63.4% of ACPI codes present in any field and showed lower variation over time compared to the principal definition. The proportion of adults with a risk factor of interest increased during the study period, particularly between 2020 and 2023. Greater than 96% of adults ≥ 65y hospitalized with ACPI in 2023 had at least one risk factor indicative for vaccination against pneumococcal, influenza, or RSV in the 3 years prior. CONCLUSIONS: We show that using only principal diagnostic codes to identify ACPI hospitalization may disproportionately inflate the decline in ACPI hospitalizations between 2014 and 2023. Using a principal ACPI hospitalization definition would exclude approximately 30% of hospitalizations that would meet the expanded principal ACPI definition. The shift towards greater use of sepsis and COPD codes in the principal diagnostic code position may be attributed to coding changes over the study period. Risk factors for pneumonia increased in prevalence, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic period.

The data source was MerativeTM MarketScan® Commercial Database with Medicare Supplement A (hereafter “MarketScan”). Included in the data are deidentified inpatient and outpatient claims for healthcare services, basic patient demographics, as well as claims for long-term care services and prescription drugs. Enrollees with Medicare supplemental insurance constituted approximately 14% of all Medicare receiving retirees in 2010 [25]. Full-year data was available for the years between January 1, 2011, and December 31, 2023.The population of interest was restricted to adults (> 18y) with at least two complete years of enrollment in MarketScan data (i.e., fully covered for more than 25 days per month and enrolled in all months of a year for at least two consecutive years). Influenza was included as part of the ACPI definition to broaden our understanding of hospitalized respiratory disease trends and address the close relationship between influenza and the development of pneumonia. Summary inpatient claims data have one principal diagnostic coding field and 14 secondary diagnostic coding fields while outpatient claims data have one principal field and four secondary fields. Diagnostic codes were classified as any position ACPI, principal ACPI (denoted 1 ̊), expanded principal ACPI (denoted 1+), and secondary only ACPI (denoted 2 ̊). Any position ACPI was the most inclusive categorization, indicating that an ICD code for ACPI was found in any of the 15 inpatient diagnostic coding fields. Principal ACPI (1 ̊) includes patients where a diagnostic code for ACPI was in the principal diagnostic coding field (DX1), regardless of codes present in secondary fields. Expanded principal ACPI (1+) encompasses individuals with a principal diagnostic code for sepsis, acute respiratory failure, meningitis, pleural empyema, or COPD, in combination with a secondary diagnostic code for ACPI or hospitalizations with a principial diagnostic code for ACPI (1 ̊). Severe cases of pneumonia may be more likely to have a principal code for meningitis, respiratory failure, and septicemia [28]. The 1 + classification also addresses changing standards by the American Hospital Association (AHA) for COPD coding when a lower respiratory infection is also present and recent research indicating that the switch from ICD-9 to ICD-10 resulted in shifts in pneumonia coding practices that allowed for higher reimbursement for respiratory failure [21, 29–31]. If a patient was hospitalized for ACPI and was a MarketScan data enrollee but had no previous inpatient or outpatient records in the three years prior to ACPI, they were recorded as having no risk factors of interest. full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionIn this descriptive study of ACPI hospitalizations, we demonstrate that the choice of diagnostic coding field criteria can influence the magnitude and direction of observed trends. The expanded principal definition of ACPI hospitalization was the more stable definition, in terms of capturing a steady proportion of total APCI codes over time, while also showing the general decline in pneumonia hospitalization between 2014 and 2023. For the 19 to 34y age group, the choice to use a principal only code to identify ACPI between 2014 and 2019 would result in a perceived decline in incidence, while the incorporation of secondary codes revealed minor increases in ACPI.Multiple shifts to coding practices occurred throughout the time period of the study which provided a unique time period to assess trends in ACPI. The first change to coding occurred in late 2015 with the switch from ICD-9 to ICD-10 in the US. Other studies have shown that the ICD-9/ICD-10 coding shift in 2015 would require an adjustment factor of approximately 7% when estimating pneumonia in adults [31]. Additionally, our data showed that the diagnostic code for COPD with LRTI (J44.0: COPD with acute LRTI) moved from the fifth most common principal diagnostic code in 2016 to the third most common in 2017. This reflects the October 2016 coding change by the AHA that required COPD to be coded in the primary position in the event of a lower respiratory tract infection with COPD although there is some room for flexibility given clinical notes for pneumonia. Previously, these hospitalization events could be coded with LRTI in the primary position and thus be captured in a principal only definition of ACPI [30, 33]. Our study also found that principal diagnoses like septicemia surpassed codes for unspecified pneumonia to be the most frequent code for ACPI hospitalization in 2017. Other studies have shown an increase in septicemia coding with one showing that between 2009 and 2014, there was a 10% increase in sepsis coding. This increase was not seen when clinical criteria alone was used to diagnose sepsis (+ 0.6%) [34]. This has been hypothesized as being due to upcoding, or the practice of prioritizing codes with higher reimbursement rates [35, 36].Our results of an increasing prevalence of underlying pneumonia risk factors among hospitalized ACPI patients are in accordance with research showing that comorbidity prevalence is increasing among adults hospitalized for pneumonia from 2020 onward. In our study, the youngest age groups, < 50y, had a higher relative increase in risk factors for pneumonia compared to older age groups, also indicating a shift in the risk profile of ACPI hospitalizations after 2020. One study comparing non-COVID-19 pneumonia hospitalizations between 2016 and 2021 showed an increase in certain chronic conditions (immunosuppression, diabetes) present among patients hospitalized during the pandemic [37–39]. This may indicate a shift in the population to those with higher susceptibility to infection during a time when non-pharmaceutical interventions were practiced and non-COVID-19 respiratory pathogen circulation was lower [40, 41]. Some of these pneumonia hospitalizations represent bacterial infections secondary to Covid-19 diagnosis, which may contribute to the higher pneumonia incidence rate and prevalence of comorbidities in pandemic period data [42, 43].
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionThis study highlights the need for standardizing pneumonia claims definitions when assessing trends over time using a US claims database. Our results provide an example of how failure to account for pneumonia coding changes, particularly the shift from principal to secondary position codes, can overestimate the decline in pneumonia over time. The expanded ACPI definition, which incorporates both principal diagnostic codes for ACPI and principal codes for COPD, empyema, meningitis, septicemia, and respiratory failure in conjunction with a secondary code for ACPI, addresses a coding shift identified around 2017 in the MarketScan database while also reflecting the decrease in ACPI incidence. Using a principal ACPI hospitalization definition would exclude approximately 30% of hospitalizations that meet the expanded principal ACPI definition, thereby excluding a proportion of severe pneumonia cases that experience sepsis, respiratory arrest, and COPD during hospitalization. Additionally, the analysis revealed that patients hospitalized with pneumonia from 2020 to 2023 had higher prevalence of underlying comorbidities than those hospitalized in years prior.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionIn 2011, all-cause pneumonia was the most frequent cause of non-childbirth-related hospitalization in the US, comprising 2.87% of all non-childbirth hospitalizations. By 2018, pneumonia had declined to the fifth leading cause, making up 2.08% of hospitalizations [1]. This decline has been attributed, in part, to the greater number and improved efficacy of respiratory vaccinations available for children and adults [2]. In the US, influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and pneumococcal vaccines are recommended for adults to prevent respiratory illnesses that can cause pneumonia and related severe diseases. Pneumococcal vaccines have been recommended to high risk adults since 1984 and influenza vaccines have been universally recommended for adults in the US since 2010 [3–5]. In 2023, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) stated that adults over 60 years of age may receive a single dose of the RSV vaccine through shared clinical decision making, with an update in 2025 expanding this recommendation to include adults 50–59 years of age at increased risk for severe RSV disease [6, 7]. Despite the increase in available respiratory vaccines to prevent respiratory infections and pre-COVID-19 pandemic declines in pneumonia hospitalizations, low vaccine uptake among adults in the US necessitates frequent assessments of trends in pneumonia hospitalization [8–10].Many risk factors for pneumonia are also indications for adult respiratory vaccination. For example, chronic lung disease, chronic kidney disease, and diabetes, are all comorbid conditions that may place an adult at greater risk for pneumococcal pneumonia, influenza, and RSV [11–13]. The prevalence of some risk factors, like chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), have remained stable in the U.S. but others, like diabetes have increased into the late 2010s and are expected to continue increasing into 2030 [14–17]. Because multimorbidity increases with increasing age, and the size of the population 65 years and older continues to grow, the absolute number of U.S. adults at risk for pneumonia are anticipated to continue to increase with time [18–20].Crucially, the reported decline in pneumonia hospitalizations is not equal across all age groups, nor is the definition of pneumonia hospitalization consistent across studies. One driver of the potential discrepancy in our understanding of trends is the method by which pneumonia is classified when analyzing medical claims data. Studies often examine International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes listed in the principal diagnostic code field, as this field is intended to capture the principal diagnosis responsible for admission. Strictly defining pneumonia by the principal code means only a portion of the total number of medical claims for inpatient pneumonia are captured [21]. Furthermore, the COVID-19 pandemic altered respiratory disease transmission cycles and social contact trends, thus affecting rates of non-COVID pneumonia hospitalizations [22]. This study aims to characterize trends in all-cause pneumonia and influenza (ACPI) hospitalization rates by diagnostic coding field position and trends in specific comorbidities among ACPI hospitalized patients pre- and post-COVID-19 pandemic. These results can aid in our understanding and predictions of future ACPI trends as new respiratory vaccines enter the market. Influenza was included as part of the ACPI definition to broaden our understanding of hospitalized respiratory disease trends and address the close relationship between influenza and the development of pneumonia. Because the study period covered the transition from ICD-9 to ICD-10 in October 2015, crosswalks for diagnostic codes were made according to forward and reverse general equivalence mapping using the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality’s (AHRQ) Map It software [27]. Summary inpatient claims data have one principal diagnostic coding field and 14 secondary diagnostic coding fields while outpatient claims data have one principal field and four secondary fields. Severe cases of pneumonia may be more likely to have a principal code for meningitis, respiratory failure, and septicemia [28].
